label: Riemannian Metrics
notes: This chapter, printed pages 327 to 348, adds the one structure smooth manifolds lack on their own: a way to measure. A Riemannian metric is a smoothly varying inner product on tangent spaces, and from it follow lengths, angles, distance, and the identification of vectors with covectors.

label: Definition of a Metric
notes: Stress that a metric is a tensor field, not a single bilinear form. At each point it is symmetric and positive definite, and smoothness means the component functions are smooth in any chart. Positive definiteness is the property that everything in the chapter ultimately depends on.

label: Local Components
notes: In a chart the metric becomes a symmetric positive-definite matrix of functions. Show that the eigenvalues are positive everywhere and that the unit ellipse, the solution set of v transpose G v equals one, is short where the metric is large. This is the workhorse picture for the whole chapter.

label: Lengths and Angles
notes: With an inner product on each tangent space, the norm and the angle formula are immediate. Emphasize that a coordinate grid that looks square on paper may be non-orthogonal in the metric: the off-diagonal entries are exactly what tilts the measured angle away from ninety degrees.

label: Length of a Curve
notes: Curve length integrates the metric speed of the velocity field. Point out reparametrization invariance, and that this single integral is the bridge from pointwise linear algebra to global geometry. The local norm under the integral sign is the only place the metric enters.

label: The Distance Function
notes: Distance is the infimum of lengths over admissible curves joining two points. Walk through symmetry, the triangle inequality, and positivity, and stress the nontrivial theorem that this distance induces the original manifold topology, proved by local comparison with the Euclidean norm.

label: Existence via Partitions of Unity
notes: Every smooth manifold admits a Riemannian metric. The proof glues Euclidean metrics pulled back from charts using a partition of unity. The key convexity fact is that a positive weighted average of positive-definite forms is positive definite, so the sum is a genuine metric.

label: Flat: Lowering Indices
notes: The flat map sends a vector to the covector obtained by feeding it into the first slot of the metric. In components this is multiplication by the matrix G, lowering an index. Because the metric is nondegenerate the flat map is an isomorphism between the tangent and cotangent spaces.

label: Sharp and the Gradient
notes: Sharp is the inverse of flat and uses the inverse metric to raise an index. The gradient of a function is the sharp of its differential, so it is metric dependent. Use the polar example where G is diag one, r squared to show the gradient is not just the tuple of partial derivatives.

label: Pullbacks and Isometries
notes: A smooth map pulls back a metric by inserting pushed-forward vectors. An isometry is a diffeomorphism whose pullback recovers the metric exactly, the right notion of equivalence for Riemannian manifolds. Pullback by an immersion is automatically a metric because injective differentials keep the Gram matrix positive definite.

label: Induced and Round Metrics
notes: Submanifolds inherit a metric by restricting the ambient one to tangent directions; the components form the Gram matrix of the Jacobian columns. Use the helicoid, whose induced metric is diag one, one plus u squared, and the round sphere as the canonical embedded examples.

label: Orthonormal Frames
notes: Gram-Schmidt applied smoothly to a local frame produces an orthonormal frame in which the metric is the identity matrix. Such frames exist on any neighborhood but generally not globally. They are the computational tool that makes many later constructions, like the volume form, clean and coordinate-free.

label: Recap and Pseudo-Riemannian Contrast
notes: Recap the chain from inner product to length to distance, and the musical maps tying TM to its dual. Close with the pseudo-Riemannian contrast: dropping positivity for mere nondegeneracy creates null vectors and breaks the length and distance theory, marking the boundary of the Riemannian world.
